#601. Rings of Power star Tyroe Muhafidin talks Theos dark side, Witch-king theories, and that heartbreaking death

Tyroe Muhafidin is ready to embrace his villainous side.

The 20-year-old actor plays Theo in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, his first professional role. A young Southlander, Theo has spent the first two seasons of the series caught up in a battle between good and evil that he can barely understand. But in Season 3, Theo hopes to take matters into his own hands, a choice that brings him face to face with Sauron (Charlie Vickers).

Over the course of Season 3's first four episodes, Theo officially joins Sauron's army as a Nazgnagôl, or Ring-servant. Later, in one of the show's heaviest scenes, he kills his former mentor, the elf Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova), at Sauron's command. Between accepting a ring of power and murdering Arondir, Theo's arc has bent entirely toward darkness, especially since the Nazgnagôl will soon become entirely corrupted, turning them into the Nazgûl of The Lord of the Rings.

In a conversation with Mashable, Muhafidin unpacked Theo's turn to the dark side, his final scene with Córdova, and whether Theo may become the Witch-king of Angmar, as the show so heavily implies.

This season, Theo gets up close and personal with Sauron. In the first episode, he and the men of Pelargir head to Mordor for a ring of power. Tell me about how the five years under Númenórean rule have led to this decision from Theo.

In the last five years, I think any of those dwindles of hope that Theo had have now all dissipated. Basically, in the first two seasons, Theo was was very hopeful for a better life, and he really did believe that something good was going to come for his people. Then it just became pain upon pain upon pain, and loss upon loss for him. Five years, especially for a human, is enough time to set in stone for him the idea that those good days weren't ever coming, and if he was ever going to have any life that's different to the one that he's having now, it would be in Barad-dûr.

That fight between the Southlanders for the ring is the most involved combat Theo's been in so far. Walk me through training for that scene and embodying that fight-or-die feeling.

I feel like I've never really done anything where I was the attacker. A lot of the stunty stuff that Theo had done prior was always him running away from something. So I feel like this is the first time, and it's showing that he's grown now, and he can take on battles for himself, full-on, headfirst.

That fight was a bit hectic. It took us a few weeks to choreograph and nail down. Adam [Basil], who's the loveliest guy ever — he's this 6-foot-8 guy, and his name on the call sheet was "Big Farmer" — was absolutely a dream to work with. He's on top of me, and you think that he would be heavy, but he did such a great job at keeping his weight just enough off me that it looked like I was holding all this weight. It was really fun, but it was really grueling to shoot. The conditions in Barad-dûr aren't the most fun. There's fire everywhere and blood everywhere, and it's dark. But I guess that's the exact vibe that Sauron's lair would have!

Speaking of Sauron, I'd love to hear more about working with Charlie Vickers this season and establishing that intriguing dynamic between Theo and Sauron.

Working with Charlie was a dream. He'd always had a particular kind of arm around me since the first season. We were all out in New Zealand by ourselves, and he'd invite me around to play FIFA with him a bunch. It was kind of like an uncle relationship, Uncle Charlie. So we already had this dynamic, and now actually working with him, we could actually build upon that kind of big bro energy.

There's been certain moments that they've shared prior, like the moment where Theo held the sword up and said, "Strength to the Southlands." Halbrand, at the time, recognized that. So, I think Sauron had an eye out for Theo. I think the moment that he stepped into Barad-dûr, her knew there was something about this kid.

I love the whole scene where Sauron uses dark magic to invite Theo to commune with his late father. What's running through Theo's mind in that moment as he learns the truth about his father and his ties to Mordor?

At this point, his mind is racing. It's so filled with everything, it would be hard for him to think rationally at all. He just did a complete fight to the death with six other guys, and now he's having to talk to the Dark Lord and meeting his dad all of a sudden, whom he hasn't known for the last 20 years. It's literally the most insane sequence of events, so at this point he's genuinely the most vulnerable, mentally. His brain is at a point now where it will soak up anything that Sauron says to him, and it has left him easy to manipulate.

Finding out who his dad was is a question that he's asked his entire life, and when he learns, it's disbelief and shock. It's one of those things where you've been wondering for so long, so when you find out, you can't believe that it's true anyway. It's this weird, in-between world of knowing now, but still feeling like he doesn't know. I think Sauron can use that uncertainty in his brain, and with the presence of a ring, it was very easy to say what needed to be said.

I have to talk about the Witch-king in the room, because Sauron tells Theo he has it in him to be a sorcerer and a king. Obviously, a very famous sorcerer king with a ring of power in The Lord of the Rings is the Witch-king of Angmar. Are you able to confirm that Theo is going down that path?

[laughs] You could theorize along those lines, maybe, but I guess you'd have to ask [co-creators] J.D. [Payne] and Patrick [McKay] about that one.

Theo puts on the ring and becomes one of the Ring-servants. When did you learn that this darkness was really going to become a part of his arc?

There was always a presence of it from the first season. With the sword hilt, there was already a connection to the dark side, and there was the scene with Waldreg [Geoff Morrell] at the watchtower trying to get him to join him. There've been temptations throughout, and they were planted carefully, so that when it came to the point that he got offered the ultimate question, he'd already been broken down gradually, and let the darkness in so much that it was easy to say yes.

I'd only found out just just before Season 3 I actually get a ring. In the five years prior to that, I'd been poking at J.D. and Patrick saying, "Will I get a ring? Will I get a ring?"

They always flipped it back on me, asking, "Should Theo get a ring?" And I was like, "I don't know. That's too much pressure!"

I did a little bit of sweet talking all the way through, saying it'd be cool to play a villain. Villain arcs are really cool, and there's some cool depth to them. Theo does have a real great sense of depth and reasoning behind his darkness.

Speaking of the rings, they all look different. Did you get a choice in which one you got to put on?

I think I got the coolest. I remember seeing them all and being like, "I hope that one's mine."

Then when I got my costume for the first time, I got to see which ring was mine, and it was exactly the one I wanted. It was my favorite one out of all of them.

We have to talk about the costume, because the image of the Nazgnagôl armor and mask recalls the Nazgûl in Lord of the Rings, and that has a lot of weight for the series. What was it like, stepping into that for the first time?

I'd done a lot of movement workshops and things like that to try and gauge a sense of the power that the Nazgnagôl would have. I'd done it for a few weeks before any kind of costume fitting, but it wasn't until the day that I had my first costume fitting — there was no armor or crown or anything, it was literally just a bunch of black robes — that I immediately could feel the darkness attached to it. You could get a sense of power, even just in the robes. Then at each costume fitting, they introduced more and more to the costume, and then by the last costume fitting, I'd fully felt the power.

I also requested if I could do some movement workshops in the costume, because it was actually really complicated to move in. The crown is essentially an extension of your head, so any movement of your head will be really exaggerated at the end of the crown. We had to figure out how to walk in a way so our heads weren't bobbing a bunch. There was a sense of trying to move like you're floating, because if we didn't do that, the crown would have just made us look goofy.

What's the secret to moving like the Nazgnagôl?

There's a sense of real strength and power, but also a sense of otherworldliness. The Nazgnagôl live in both the mortal life and the immortal life, so we wanted them to move as if they were in between worlds, and they're coming from one world to another. It was very much about moving with a slight bend at the knees, so every time you're moving, it's more of a glide than a walk. I think once the costume's on, though, it does 80 percent of the work for you. You just automatically feel it.

It's very imposing. We've got to talk about the final scene of episode 4, with Arondir's death. Tell me about filming that final scene with Ismael and finding that last connection?

We shot that scene over two weeks, so we'd shot that specific sequence and the stabbing multiple times without getting any close up. We'd done it wide a bunch of times, and every point up until then, we were really light-hearted. We were having fun on set, and then the day came where we were doing our close-ups, and the air just felt cold, and everyone could feel the sad energy. It was so heavily emotional, like for both of us, it was a real bonding and brotherhood moment. We got a lot closer, because we could open up on our feelings. Feeling so deeply at that time in that moment, it really opened up a big space for us to connect. It was fun though. We had a really great time, and it was a really great group of us on set. It was daunting, but it was very fun. It was a big celebration of Ismael and all the hard work that he's put into this job and how awesome Arondir is. I'm so glad that he got to do all this really cool shit at the end.

What was your reaction to first reading that Theo stabs him?

I knew beforehand. I think initially J.D. and Patrick's plan was to wait for me to just get the script and read it, but Charlotte Brandstrom, the first episode director, just blurted it out to me. I was like, "Oh, I guess that was the whole secret they were trying to keep from me."

So, I knew it was coming, but I didn't know how. I knew at some point if I was going to go to the dark side, there would be a confrontation between them, because obviously they're fighting on opposing ends of the war, and they're both frontmen. Reading it, I just didn't imagine it to be as heartfelt as it was. I always thought that it was going to be a lot colder and a lot quicker. So, reading it and seeing how close he was to really accepting Arondir was really heartbreaking. This is actually such a love-filled scene, and that's why it's so tragic and so heartbreaking, because there is so much love between them, and it just disappears in an instant, which leaves a real hollow feeling at the end of the episode.

There's that moment of compulsion from Sauron that makes Theo stab Arondir. What's he thinking at that moment? Is he reevaluating his choice, or is his humanity too far gone?

Theo is definitely someone who's been a product of who his role models are and who is giving him guidance. This is the moment where his two biggest role models in his life at this point are meeting head to head. For the last few weeks, Theo has been under the influence of Sauron. He has been fed however many ideas in his head about the elves. But then when he sees Arondir's face, all those ideas that Sauron had planted disappear, and he's almost ready to accept the hand that's put out in front of him because he can see the the love in Arondir's eyes. That moment when Sauron arrives is him thinking, "Oh yeah, I remember what I'm supposed to be doing now." It flips back into work mode, or servant mode.

Right now we know the Nazgnagôl as Ring-servants, but we know that the final iteration of them is the Nazgûl, who are totally far gone. Assuming Theo stays on this path, what is an element of that transformation that you're most excited to play?

The cool thing about the Nazgnagôl and the Nazgûl is that they have a completely different living experience to anything else in Middle-earth. They are living in between two worlds, and so you're trying to explore what it looks like to be detaching from the mortal world, becoming more spirit-like, and losing a sense of reality while being completely controlled and manipulated. It'll be really interesting because at this point in time, the Nazgnagôl are still men. They have autonomy over themselves and their decisions and what they can do, whereas it'd be great to see them slowly not be able to do that.

The show has such a massive array of locations to visit. Going forward, what is one of the worlds within Middle-earth that you would like to work in?

I would love, love, love to do work in Númenor. The sets are just so magnificent. Everything around it is so glorious and beautiful, and there's a real community vibe. Any time I've been on the sets with the Númenóreans, they all seem to be getting along real well, whereas I've been hanging out with orcs who most of the time aren't that happy. [laughs]

And who is someone from the ensemble you'd love to work with?

I'd love to do work with more or at least more stuff with Leon [Wadham], who plays Kemen. I really wish we had more to do. I love Leon. When we were shooting Season 3, he was actually living above me, so we were constantly just borrowing stuff off each other all the time and just talking about work or whatever. We only ever had two days on set, and it was the last scene of Season 2 and the first scene of Season 3. But I also just think Kemen is not a nice guy.

Every time he's on screen, I'm angry. I don't even care if Theo's on the dark side. He deserves his vengeance a little.

Yeah, I'd love for Theo to face off against Kemen and give him what he deserves.

#600. Pete Hegseth Is About to Get His Ass Kicked

It’s been one week since Election Day, and Pete Hegseth is facing a different kind of war. Trump administration officials tell Inner Loop they knew the defense secretary would face a slew of investigations in the next Congress. Now, they think he is on track to be Democrats’ number one target—and Democrats are already planning to make their case as airtight as possible.

“Hegseth is now a passenger in whatever comes next,” says one source close to President Donald Trump. “And all the outcomes are potentially damaging.”

House Democratic aides tell Inner Loop that Democrats are likely to pursue an impeachment inquiry against Hegseth, and also work to narrow the charges against him to issues that Senate Republicans have also complained about, in an effort to attract their support.

Hegseth, who has championed the deeply unpopular and costly Iran war, has spent much of his controversial tenure upending various internal processes at the Defense Department, including firing generals and blocking promotions using criteria that disproportionately affected women and people of color. He has also become known for his notorious role in Signalgate and for military strikes against purported drug traffickers in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean.

Some of those topics have also previously been the subject of complaints from Republicans. The Senate Armed Services Committee chair Roger Wicker criticized Hegseth for the flag officer cuts and once reportedly threatened to block a Trump nominee unless the Pentagon handed over documents.

Last night, House Republicans managed to table an impeachment effort targeting Hegseth that was brought about by Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky. Massie, among other issues, accused Hegseth of waging the Iran war without approval from Congress and directing “extrajudicial killings.” But even though the effort failed, officials privately believe it is practically inevitable that Hegseth will be impeached again and face a Senate trial next year.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries suggested as much after the impeachment failed to progress, telling reporters he would consult with his top members on next steps.

“We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time, and that’ll be led by Adam Smith, soon to be chair of the Armed Services Committee, and Jamie Raskin, next chair of the judiciary,” Jeffries said.

Trump officials tell Inner Loop they still don’t expect Democrats to get enough GOP support to remove Hegseth—but they can’t shield him from wall-to-wall coverage of a trial.

The impeachment articles brought by Massie were seen by some Republicans as overly broad, which made officials think they could spare Hegseth an impeachment trial by having Senate majority leader John Thune dismiss all the charges in a straight-line vote.

But with Democrats taking over the Senate next year, that option is off the table.

It’s not going to be entirely simple, however. Hegseth’s biggest Republican detractors are all leaving Congress at the end of the year. Maine senator Susan Collins, North Carolina senator Thom Tillis, and Louisiana senator Bill Cassidy all lost reelection this midterm cycle, while Iowa senator Joni Ernst and Kentucky senator Mitch McConnell are stepping down after finishing their terms.

But even with his biggest detractors set to retire, at least five other Republican senators have complained about Hegseth’s performance—getting Democrats closer to the 67 votes needed to convict—like Wicker, South Dakota senator Mike Rounds, Kentucky senator Rand Paul, Alaska senator Lisa Murkowski, and Indiana senator Todd Young.

This is why the focus of the Democratic impeachment inquiry is going to have to be specific, and geared to Republican interests, so as to be unassailable.

Hegseth, for what it’s worth, doesn’t seem to want to go anywhere without a fight. In a televised appearance at the Pentagon earlier this week, Hegseth responded to a question about Vice President JD Vance blaming the Republican midterm losses on Iran, and said Vance was a “critical member of the team” and the war effort.

Hegseth then added, “I agree with what the president said, when he said ‘Hey, if I had to do this all over again, would we do it again? Absolutely.’”

​House Republicans are poised to open an investigation into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's interactions with alleged Chinese spy and one-time tech executive Alice Huang, who is not related to the CEO.

The growing push for Congress to stand up its own investigation is set to put Republicans on a collision course with Trump, who has continued to publicly defend the CEO of the world's most valuable chip company.

During a congressional “Gang of Eight” briefing on Monday, officials including director of national intelligence Jay Clayton and CIA director John Ratcliffe gave only the broad brushstrokes of the classified intelligence surrounding Huang’s interactions, which left lawmakers deeply unsatisfied, sources say.

Meeting attendees did not get clear answers as to why there was no defensive briefing provided to Jensen Huang and whether he was initially left off Trump's trip to China this year as a result of the possible national security risk.

On Tuesday, the chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Brian Mast, told reporters he would be open to issuing a subpoena to compel Jensen Huang to provide a briefing behind closed doors if he ignored a request from last week to appear on Capitol Hill.

Mast, together with Rick Crawford, the chair of the House Intelligence Committee, and John Moolenaar, the chair of the China select subcommittee, had asked Jensen Huang to appear before the three panels later this month.

The congressional inquiry follows revelations from The New York Times that secretary of state Marco Rubio drafted a memo for Trump warning that classified intelligence suggested Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security. China has denied any espionage allegations.

SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.

Starship is scheduled to launch on its 15th test flight today from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). SpaceX plans to bring both of Starship's stages back to Starbase for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — something it has never done before.

You can watch it all live here at Space.com. And there should be a lot to see: Starship Flight 15 will last more than 22 hours, if all goes according to plan.

Starship consists of two elements: a huge booster known as Super Heavy and an upper-stage spacecraft called Starship, or Ship for short. Both are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first in the world of orbital spaceflight.

The rapidity of Starship's reuse hinges heavily on SpaceX's recovery strategy: Returning both vehicles directly to the launch mount will enable much faster inspection, refurbishment and reflight, the company has said.

SpaceX has already caught Super Heavy, pulling the feat off on three previous Starship test flights. But it has never tried to do so with Ship, which flies farther and faster than the booster and is therefore a more challenging vehicle to recover.

So today's flight is a pretty big deal for SpaceX.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," the company wrote in a Flight 15 mission description.

The action will unspool over two days, if all goes to plan. Super Heavy will return to Starbase for a touchdown just 6.5 minutes after launch, but Ship will continue on to low Earth orbit.

The upper stage will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites, during a 42-minute stretch beginning about 35 minutes after liftoff. This will be just the second batch of V3 spacecraft to reach orbit, after the 26 that went up on Flight 14 on Sept. 28.

Ship will then stay aloft for nearly a full day. The mission plan calls for the upper stage to return to Starbase for its chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), about 22.5 hours after liftoff.

There's no guarantee things will go according to plan, however. SpaceX will call off a Ship catch if the vehicle experiences any issues during Flight 15. If something crops up, the company will steer Ship to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, either near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

So it'll be a busy weekend for SpaceX, and for space fans who want to keep tabs on the mission. And we can help you out there, with our Flight 15 updates page.

#597. A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness

A powerful new computer simulation is allowing scientists to explore one of the most mysterious periods in cosmic history, when the universe emerged from darkness and the first stars and galaxies began to transform the cosmos.

Developed by researchers at MIT, Harvard University, and other institutions, the simulation, called Lumina, recreates the evolution of the early universe across a region roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide. It follows 2 billion years of cosmic history, revealing how galaxies formed, how radiation spread through space, and how the universe gradually became transparent to light.

The research, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), provides an unusually detailed picture of events that unfolded billions of years before our solar system existed.

How the Universe Entered Its Cosmic Dark Age

The story begins with the Big Bang, when the universe existed in an extremely hot, dense state filled with electrons and other subatomic particles. This primordial plasma, described as initially smaller than a single atom, expanded rapidly and cooled as the universe grew.

Eventually, particles slowed enough for electrons to combine with atomic nuclei, producing electrically neutral hydrogen. Around 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe entered a period known as the cosmic "dark age."

Although the universe had become transparent to much of the radiation left over from the Big Bang, stars had not yet formed to illuminate the cosmos. Neutral hydrogen filled space and could absorb certain types of radiation, including the ultraviolet light that would later emerge from the first stars.

Lumina allows researchers to investigate how this early environment evolved, eventually giving rise to the galaxies, stars, and other structures that helped bring the dark age to an end.

How the First Stars and Black Holes Transformed the Universe

The simulation covers an immense region measuring 500 megaparsecs, equivalent to approximately 1.6 billion light-years. Within that volume, Lumina follows dark matter, gas, stars, and radiation (such as photons), capturing both the behavior of matter across enormous distances and the formation of individual galaxies.

One of its most important achievements is recreating two major changes in the early universe: hydrogen re-ionization and helium re-ionization.

Hydrogen re-ionization began as the first stars and galaxies produced increasing amounts of ultraviolet radiation. This energetic light removed electrons from neutral hydrogen atoms, a process called "re-ionizing" the gas. As more hydrogen became ionized, the universe became increasingly transparent to ultraviolet light, allowing radiation to travel across much greater distances.

This transformation helped clear the widespread neutral hydrogen that had dominated the early cosmos. Lumina reproduces the process in remarkable detail, showing how radiation from the first generations of stars gradually changed the conditions throughout space.

The simulation also follows helium re-ionization, which requires substantially more energetic radiation to strip electrons from helium.

The results point to different sources driving these two transformations. Early stars and galaxies appear to have been primarily responsible for ionizing hydrogen, while actively feeding supermassive black holes supplied the intense radiation needed to ionize helium.

This is the first simulation to capture both processes together, offering a more complete view of how the early universe changed.

"Lumina does everything from small-scale star and galaxy formation to large-scale reionization of hydrogen and helium, in a volume that is 100 times larger than previous best simulations," says study author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT.

The researchers are making Lumina available to other scientists, allowing its predictions about early cosmic structures to be compared with observations from existing and future telescopes. Such comparisons could help researchers better understand the events that shaped the first galaxies and stars.

Building a Virtual Universe With Half a Trillion Elements

Lumina gets its name from the Latin word meaning "lights." Its underlying technology builds on IllustrisTNG, an earlier simulation developed by scientists at MIT and other institutions, including members of the Lumina research team.

IllustrisTNG models how galaxies form and evolve by following the interactions of dark matter, gas, and other physical processes from the Big Bang to the present day.

To create Lumina, researchers upgraded the existing software so it could reproduce galaxy formation in comparable detail across a much larger region of space. They also incorporated a radiation transport model that calculates how light, including ultraviolet radiation, travels through the universe and interacts with surrounding matter.

Together, these improvements allow the simulation to track both the formation of galaxies and the enormous changes that radiation produces across cosmic distances.

The resulting model contains approximately half a trillion individual elements, including particles of dark matter and cells representing gas. It provides roughly 30 times the resolution of IllustrisTNG while covering a region 100 times larger in volume than previous leading simulations.

Recreating billions of years of interactions across so many elements requires extraordinary computing resources. The researchers used Frontier, one of the world's most powerful supercomputers, located at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

"At peak scale, the calculation brings together the equivalent of more than 100,000 CPU cores and around 15,000 GPUs," says Xuejian (Jacob) Shen, an MIT co-author of the study. "Making all of those processors communicate efficiently while continuously evolving trillions of interacting pieces of information is itself an extraordinary feat of computer engineering."

Watching the First Galaxies Emerge From Darkness

Lumina begins approximately 45 million years after the Big Bang, during an era when neutral hydrogen dominated the universe.

Researchers initialized the simulation using conditions based on scientists' understanding of that period. They then allowed the model to calculate how gas and dark matter interacted throughout its half a trillion elements as cosmic time progressed.

At the same time, Lumina tracked how radiation appeared, spread, and interacted with matter, including the ultraviolet light produced by emerging stars.

The result is a virtual universe that scientists can explore at dramatically different scales, from the arrangement of matter across enormous cosmic distances down to the development of a single galaxy.

On the project website, the researchers have released videos showing these processes in action. One offers a "zoom-in" from the entire simulated region to an individual disk-shaped galaxy. Another presents a time-lapse of the complete volume, showing how hydrogen re-ionization spreads across the universe over 2 billion years.

"On the one hand, it's evolving dark matter as well as the gas in the universe, and on the other, it's also tracking how radiation travels," Zier explains. "We see dark matter and gas start to clump in these over-densities. And when we zoom in, we can see gas is falling into these dark matter haloes. Zooming in more, we see this is where the first galaxies form. And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen."

This ability to move between vastly different scales is one of Lumina's defining strengths. Researchers can examine the formation of individual galaxies while also observing how their combined radiation affects the universe on a much larger scale.

"Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," Vogelsberger notes. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation."

A New Way to Explore the Universe's Earliest History

The research team plans to use Lumina to investigate the large-scale arrangement of matter in the early universe. The simulation could also help predict the patterns of gravitational waves generated by ancient galaxies and black holes.

Another major opportunity will come from comparing Lumina's virtual universe with real observations. New and upcoming telescopes are expected to collect increasingly detailed information about enormous numbers of distant galaxies, providing scientists with fresh ways to test their understanding of the early cosmos.

Because Lumina simulates such a large volume of space, it can generate extensive populations of galaxies that can be directly compared with these observations.

"One of Lumina's major advantages is its sheer size," Shen says. "It produces enormous populations of simulated galaxies, finally allowing us to make comparisons with the very large galaxy samples that upcoming surveys will observe."

By bringing together detailed galaxy formation, dark matter, gas, and the movement of radiation, Lumina offers researchers a powerful new tool for reconstructing the universe's earliest chapters. It may help explain not only how the first galaxies took shape, but also how their stars and black holes transformed the surrounding cosmos.

The study's MIT authors include Mark Vogelsberger, Xuejian (Jacob) Shen, and Teodora-Elena Bluichi. Other contributors include first author Oliver Zier (a former postdoc in the Vogelsberger Lab), Rongrong Liu, Sonja Koehler, and Lars Hernquist of the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics; Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas; Rahul Kannan of York University in Canada; and Volker Springel and Rüdiger Pakmor of the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics in Germany.

The research received partial support from NASA and the National Science Foundation. It also used computing resources at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which is supported by the Advanced Scientific Computing Research programs within the Office of Science at the U.S. Department of Energy.

#595. Voyager 1 is about to hit one light-day away. NASAs planning to party.

If you step outside tonight and flick a flashlight toward deep space, that split-second pulse will race through the void at 186,000 miles per second.

The light will continue its journey while you sleep, while you eat, while you go to work. Only when you reach the same time tomorrow could its photons potentially wash over a spacecraft more than 16 billion miles away.

That robotic probe is NASA's Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object in the universe. It will cross the one light-day-away milestone at 5:16 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 18. One light-day is the distance light travels over 24 hours. Radio signals move at the speed of light, so any message from Earth would need a full day to reach the spacecraft. Considering Voyager 1 never stops moving, that communication lag will only increase.

To mark the occasion, the U.S. space agency has a couple of things planned, one of which involves pointing that flashlight toward the sky. The day after the milestone, you can watch the mission team talk about where the spacecraft has been and how it keeps going.

Voyager 1 left Earth in 1977 to explore the giant outer planets. NASA timed the launch to catch a lineup of those planets that comes around only once every 176 years. The probe finished its tour decades ago but kept going at nearly 38,000 mph. In 2012, it left the heliosphere, the protective bubble the sun blows around our solar system, and entered interstellar space.

Its twin, Voyager 2, took a different path past Uranus and Neptune and left the solar system in 2018. But Voyager 2 won't reach a light-day until November 2035, most likely after it has depleted its fuel.

That's the bittersweet reality of Voyager 1's historic achievement: Both probes are dying, nearly tapped out of their nuclear power sources that turn heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. Since 2024, the team has shut off two science instruments on each spacecraft to stretch what's left. Sooner or later, the power will run out, and no one will be able to talk with the twins at all, regardless of time delays.

For now, though, the mission team is only thinking happy thoughts. The first way to get involved comes after sunset on Tuesday, Nov. 17. NASA is asking people around the world to point a light at the sky to spell out VGR, Voyager's call sign, in Morse code. Morse code is an old telegraph language that turns each letter into a pattern of short and long signals.

The easiest way to do this is with a phone or tablet. NASA built an online flasher that blinks the code for you. After sunset, open the flasher in your device's web browser, point the device's screen at the sky, and let it send the signal. (You can bookmark this story to keep the flasher link handy.)

If you'd rather tap it out yourself, grab a flashlight, and switch it on and off or use your hand to block and unblock the beam. Short flashes, called dots, should last less than a second. Long flashes, called dashes, should last about one second.

You can repeat the pattern as many times as you like.

Now, even if you were to point your flashlight in precisely the direction of Voyager 1, the beam would fan out into a cone billions of miles wide, scattering its photons across the void. Because the light is diluted in space, virtually every photon would sail past the tiny 12-foot spacecraft without ever hitting it.

But it's a symbolic gesture for wishing the old mission godspeed. You can tag @NASA on your photos and videos if you post them to X, Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, or other social media.

The second way to join in the celebration comes at noon ET / 9 a.m. PT on Thursday, Nov. 19. Mission leaders and top NASA science officials will meet at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California to talk about the twins. They'll explain how the spacecraft are holding up, what they're still learning beyond the sun's bubble, and how engineers keep such old hardware running from far away. The public can watch on NASA's streaming service, NASA+, or Youtube.

The team has plenty to talk about. This year, engineers tried a fix they nicknamed the "Big Bang." They turned off three power-hungry devices on each probe that help keep it warm, and at the same time they switched on three lower-power replacements. The swap should keep them running for at least another year.

But at this stage, the team has come to expect the unexpected. Last month, Voyager 1 had a mysterious issue with its thrusters that briefly caused a communication blackout. Engineers are still trying to figure out what caused the problem.

If the distant spacecraft could send you a Morse code message back, perhaps it would say the one recorded on its Golden Record: "ad astera per aspera." In Latin, that means "to the stars through struggles."

#593. NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade

Unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, reaching one of its largest sizes on record. Despite the striking increase, scientists from NASA and NOAA say Earth's protective ozone layer is continuing its gradual recovery and remains on track to heal later this century.

The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area. Scientists attributed the expansion primarily to an exceptionally strong polar vortex, a large circulation of winds that influences atmospheric conditions over Antarctica. They also emphasized that international efforts to reduce harmful chemicals have prevented the hole from becoming even larger.

Between September 7 and October 13, 2026, when ozone depletion was at its seasonal peak, the hole covered an average of approximately 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers). That is more than twice the size of the United States. Scientists closely monitor ozone in the stratosphere because it serves as Earth's natural "sunscreen," protecting living organisms from dangerous solar radiation. Unlike this beneficial layer high in the atmosphere, ozone near Earth's surface is a pollutant frequently associated with human activities.

Antarctica's Ozone Hole Reaches Its Largest Size in a Decade

The ozone hole reached its maximum extent on September 18, spreading across 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). This was approximately 90% of the size of the largest ozone hole ever measured, which occurred on September 9, 2000.

"The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing," said Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland and longtime leader of NASA's ozone research team at the agency's Goddard Space Flight Center. "But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven't seen in a decade."

Although the hole expanded to an extraordinary size, the results also demonstrate the benefits of decades of international environmental protections. Without reductions in chemicals known to destroy ozone, the affected area could have been substantially greater.

"The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak," Newman said.

How a Powerful Polar Vortex Accelerates Ozone Loss

Ozone depletion begins with chemicals released through human activities, particularly compounds containing chlorine and bromine. Atmospheric circulation transports these substances into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet radiation breaks them apart. The released chlorine and bromine atoms then participate in chemical reactions involving particles in Antarctic stratospheric clouds, leading to the destruction of ozone.

A major factor in this process is the stratospheric polar vortex, a seasonal band of strong winds that circles Antarctica. This circulation traps extremely cold air over the region, allowing the formation of the special clouds that help trigger ozone destruction. When the vortex becomes unusually strong or expansive, conditions favorable for ozone loss can persist across a larger area.

In 2026, atmospheric disturbances that would normally weaken the vortex were unusually subdued. This allowed the circulation to remain powerful and helped create a broader region where ozone could be destroyed.

"The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September," said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. "That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the South Pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur."

NASA and NOAA Measure the 2026 Ozone Hole

Despite its exceptional geographic size, the 2026 ozone hole did not experience the same extreme levels of ozone loss observed during record-breaking events 10 or 20 years earlier.

To measure ozone concentrations, NOAA researchers launched instruments attached to weather balloons from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory. They also collected readings using the Dobson Ozone Spectrophotometer, an optical device designed to measure atmospheric ozone. Their observations showed that ozone levels directly above the South Pole fell to their lowest reading of 2026 on October 17, reaching 105 Dobson units.

The Dobson unit is the standard measurement used to describe the total amount of ozone above a particular location. To illustrate the scale, 100 Dobson units would produce a layer of ozone just 1 millimeter thick, approximately the thickness of a dime, if all the ozone in the atmospheric column were compressed to standard temperature and pressure at sea level. The lowest ozone concentration ever measured over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units in October 2006.

Satellites provide another essential source of information. Since 1979, spaceborne instruments have helped scientists observe changes in the ozone layer and track its condition over time. The 2026 measurements included data from NASA's Aura satellite, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, a joint NASA and NOAA mission.

Why Earth's Ozone Layer Is Still Recovering

Scientists say the latest observations reinforce evidence that international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals are working. Much of that progress can be traced to the Montreal Protocol, a global agreement adopted in 1987 to phase out substances responsible for damaging the ozone layer.

Under the agreement, countries committed to replacing harmful compounds such as chlorofluorocarbons with alternatives that pose less danger to atmospheric ozone. According to Stephen Montzka, a senior scientist at NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory, chlorine concentrations in the Antarctic stratosphere associated with ozone-depleting chemicals have declined by approximately one-third compared with their peak levels in the 1980s.

These reductions are significant because chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting compounds were once common in refrigerators, air conditioning systems, building insulation, and other everyday products. Although many of these substances have been phased out, they can remain in the atmosphere for decades. Additional emissions can also occur when older equipment, materials, and landfill waste release chemicals that were manufactured years ago.

Because these compounds break down so slowly, repairing the ozone layer takes many decades. Nevertheless, continued monitoring by NASA and NOAA indicates that the long-term recovery is progressing. Even with unusually large seasonal ozone holes such as the one observed in 2026, scientists expect the Antarctic ozone hole to recover by the 2070s.

The latest findings illustrate how exceptional atmospheric conditions can temporarily produce severe ozone depletion without reversing decades of environmental progress. They also highlight the lasting impact of international cooperation in protecting Earth's atmosphere.

#590. Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water

Earth may have created a substantial amount of its own water as the planet was forming, rather than relying entirely on comets, meteorites, or other objects to deliver it from space. New research published in Nature Geoscience suggests that chemical reactions between rocky pebbles and the hydrogen-rich atmosphere of the young Earth could have produced enormous quantities of water.

The discovery offers a new explanation for how our planet acquired one of the most important ingredients for life. It also raises the possibility that other rocky planets throughout the universe could generate water through similar processes, potentially making habitable worlds more common than previously thought.

Researchers at The University of New Mexico investigated this possibility by recreating some of the extreme conditions that existed during Earth's formation. The study was led by graduate student Susmita Garai, along with Zachary Sharp, professor and director of Earth and Planetary Sciences, and Peter Olson. Their experiments examined what happens when rocks containing iron react with hydrogen at extremely high temperatures.

"Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites. Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism," explained Sharp. "In order to evaluate the possibility of 'pebble' rain' being a source of water, we needed to construct and execute some very challenging high-temperature experiments. Dr. Garai's efforts paid off mightily, as she found that water is produced in just minutes in the high temperature environment of the Early Earth's atmosphere."

A New Explanation for the Origin of Earth's Water

For decades, scientists have debated where Earth's water originally came from. One prominent theory suggests that much of it was transported to the developing planet by icy material originating in the colder, more distant regions of the early solar system.

According to this explanation, water-rich objects, including small icy pebbles, traveled inward and eventually contributed to Earth's water supply. However, researchers have struggled to fully explain how enough of this material could have reached our planet from such great distances. There are also unresolved questions about whether this delivery process accounts for Earth's chemical composition.

The new study investigates a different route by which water could have appeared. Instead of arriving already contained in ice or other materials, water may have been produced directly through reactions involving the rocky ingredients that built Earth and the gases surrounding it.

During the planet's earliest stages, countless small pieces of rock gradually came together to form a larger body. Scientists refer to this growth process as pebble accretion. As Earth gained mass, it could have accumulated a dense atmosphere containing large amounts of hydrogen, with temperatures and pressures far higher than those found on the planet today.

Under those conditions, rocky pebbles falling through the atmosphere could have triggered a remarkable chemical reaction. Hydrogen in the surrounding gas would react with iron oxide inside the silicate rocks, transforming the iron oxide into metallic iron while releasing water vapor.

Experiments Reveal Water Can Form in Minutes

To determine whether this process could actually occur, the researchers exposed samples of silicate rock to temperatures ranging from 1,200 to 1,400 degrees Celsius. They conducted experiments using flowing hydrogen gas and repeated the tests with helium to provide a comparison. Each experiment ran for between 15 minutes and three hours.

The results provided strong evidence that the proposed reaction works under these extreme conditions. When the rocks were heated in hydrogen, almost 80% of their iron oxide was transformed into metallic iron, with water vapor produced during the reaction.

In contrast, the researchers did not observe the same reaction when helium was used instead of hydrogen. This difference confirmed that hydrogen played a crucial role in generating the water.

The speed and scale of the reaction were especially striking. Although the scientists had expected some water to form, the results suggested that the process could have been far more productive than anticipated. When they extended their experimental findings to conditions on the early Earth, their calculations indicated that the mechanism might have generated hundreds of oceans' worth of water.

"We had suspected and hoped that we would produce iron metal and water in our reduction experiments, but we really had no way of knowing how fast and how much. We were quite surprised to find that extrapolation of our work suggests that hundreds of oceans' worth of water were likely produced in this way. Looking out over a large body of water, it is hard to imagine that that water may have been produced 4 ½ billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere, but it very well may have," said Sharp.

Earth's Fiery Beginnings May Have Helped Create Its Oceans

These findings suggest that the conditions of Earth's formation may have actively contributed to its water supply. Rather than being entirely dependent on water delivered from elsewhere in the solar system, the growing planet may have possessed the ingredients needed to manufacture water through its own chemical reactions.

The implications extend well beyond Earth. If rocky planets around other stars develop similarly hot, hydrogen-rich atmospheres during their formation, they might also produce substantial amounts of water as rocky material accumulates.

This possibility could have important consequences for understanding how common water is across the universe. A process that naturally occurs during the formation of Earth-sized planets would mean that obtaining water might not require the right icy objects to arrive from distant regions of a planetary system.

Could Other Earth-Like Planets Make Their Own Water?

The research also adds to growing interest in pebble accretion as an explanation for how planets form. Although the concept has gained attention relatively recently, it has already helped scientists address several longstanding questions about planetary development.

"The idea of pebble accretion is still relatively new. It's only been around for the last decade. But it seems to solve many problems that exist with the existing paradigm for planet formation," Sharp said. "And now we see that it also can explain why our planet is habitable. By extension, it is reasonable to expect that other Earth-sized bodies circling other stars would also have water and possibly life."

There are still important uncertainties to resolve. While the experiments show that rocky material can generate water when exposed to hydrogen under conditions resembling those of the early Earth, they do not establish how much of our planet's present water supply was actually produced this way. Additional research will be needed to determine the contribution of this mechanism compared with water delivered by comets, meteorites, and other sources.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important process that may have shaped Earth billions of years ago. They also suggest that the ability to produce water could be built into the formation of rocky planets themselves, opening new possibilities for understanding where water, and perhaps life, might exist beyond our solar system.

Materials provided by University of New Mexico. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#589. The Best Early Black Friday MacBook Air Deal: $200 Off

Well ahead of Black Friday, the MacBook Air is already $200 off, bringing down the price of the 13-inch model with an M5 chip, 16 GB of RAM, and 512 GB of storage to $1,099.

This is the lowest price the MacBook Air has been at since June, when Apple permanently hiked prices across its entire Mac lineup. Amazon frequently sells this MacBook Air for $1,149, but this even lower price is usually reserved for big sales events—the last being in October during Prime Day. And now it's back.

I probably don't need to expound too much on what makes the M5 MacBook Air such a fantastic, do-it-all laptop. It's extremely well-built, the performance and battery life are both top-notch, and it's still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. There's a reason it tops my list of laptop recommendations—even after having tested dozens of new models this year.

Unlike the MacBook Neo, which makes compromises on memory and performance to achieve its low price, the MacBook Air does nearly everything right. And while a MacBook Pro may tempt you—whether the new M6 model or one of the more powerful touchscreen OLED models—most people won't actually feel the difference in performance. Unless content creation, media, or game development is a full-time gig for you, I think you'll be surprised by just how much the M5 MacBook Air can handle.

The only real question is what size is right for you. The 13-inch model plays to the strengths of the MacBook Air—offering an extremely portable laptop at a reasonable price without sacrificing performance. If you would appreciate a larger screen (and don’t plan to travel with the device as much), you might prefer the 15-inch model, which is also $200 off its retail price, currently selling for $1,299. Aside from the larger screen, the only other difference is a much more robust six-speaker audio system.

Either way, now remains a really good time to buy a MacBook Air. While prices were certainly lower in the first half of 2026, we’re still probably many months out from the inevitable M6 refresh. I don’t claim to have any insider knowledge, but based on pricing history, I can’t see these laptops coming down any lower in price over the next few months.

#588. The 12 best phones of 2026, tested by experts

After extensive testing, we're ready to name the best smartphones of 2026, and we don't take these recommendations lightly.

For most of us, our phone is the most important device we own. It's a lifeline to friends and family, and our primary gateway to the internet. And unless you're still carrying around a separate camera, your phone is also your means of documenting the world around you. There's a lot riding on this pocket-sized gadget!

Mashable has been covering smartphones since 2011, and we've tested all of this year's most exciting releases so far, including the latest flagships and foldables from Apple, Samsung, and Google. Phones have definitely gotten more expensive this year, but we have recommendations for every budget across both iOS and Android operating systems.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

If you're in the market for a new phone right now, you should know that it'll cost you more than usual. The best phones were never cheap, but smartphone prices surged in 2026 amid a global RAM shortage driven by the AI boom (commonly known as "RAMageddon"). New AI data centers are hogging supplies of memory and SSD storage chips, driving up their prices. Consequently, consumer tech devices with memory components are also getting more expensive. (RAMageddon price hikes have also taken a toll on laptops and gaming consoles.)

So far, we've seen Apple, Google, and Samsung all raise the prices of their new smartphones at launch. This fall, Samsung implemented another $100 to $200 price hike across its Galaxy S26 lineup, while Apple increased the prices of some older iPhones by $100. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

With this in mind, it's especially wise to shop around for deals and carrier promotions before buying your new phone. Trading in an older device is the easiest way to save several hundred dollars on an upgrade. Some carriers will give you a new phone for free (in the form of monthly bill credits) if you also sign up for a new line or certain data plans. For example, the new iPhone 18 Pro is free with eligible trade-ins and plans through AT&T and T-Mobile.

Want to learn more about getting the best out of your tech? Sign up for Mashable's Top Stories and Deals newsletters or get Mashable push alerts today.

The average iOS user: Most people will be perfectly happy with the regular iPhone. Fast, long-lasting, pretty, and equipped with nice cameras, it's the Goldilocks of Apple handsets — not too basic, but not overkill.

Impatient folks: The Pro-level iPhone just got an upgrade, but the iPhone 18 probably isn't launching until March 2027. If you can't wait until then, last year's iPhone 17 is still a rock-solid buy.

Read Mashable's full review of the Apple iPhone 17.

Apple didn't reinvent the wheel with this one — we might get a more dramatic redesign next year — but the iPhone 17 is an awesome smartphone nonetheless. In fact, "It's easily the most compelling standard iPhone in years," per Mashable senior editor Stan Schroeder. As he pointed out in his review, it's basically an iPhone 17 Pro with no telephoto lens, vapor chamber cooling system, or RAW video support. (That's the extent of their tangible differences that we noticed in testing, but I'll add that the regular iPhone also lacks a 1TB storage option.) If you're not a specialty user in dire need of those features, it just makes sense to go with Apple's mid-range phone. For a couple of hundred dollars less than a Pro model, you still get a buttery 120Hz display, stellar performance and battery life, and very capable main cameras with the iPhone 17. Its wider range of colors and less bulky, less polarizing design seals the deal.

The average Android user: If you're happily part of team Android, then Google makes some of the best phones in the mobile market. Google's latest flagship phone is largely the same device as its Pro-tier models (save for some even better cameras and an underwhelming LED notification system), but it comes in safely under $1,000. Out of all the Android phones we've tried, this one strikes the happiest medium between value and features.

Parents: The Pixel 11 has a new Magic Capture camera feature that automatically takes and edits photos when you're recording video. Instead of trying to capture both at once or wrangle fast-moving kiddos for a picture, you can stay in the moment.

Read Mashable's full review of the Google Pixel 11.

The new Google Pixel 11 proves that you can get everything you need in an Android phone for under $1,000.

Google fine-tuned its flagship phone with a thinner design and a newer, faster chipset for 2026. Like Apple's regular iPhone, it's still a very slick smartphone even though it's not an exciting gen-over-gen upgrade. And also like Apple's regular iPhone, it has a lot in common with its pricier Pro-tier counterpart. Better cameras and a sharper display with an anti-scratch coating are the biggest things you get for splurging. (The two phones have the same processor, form factor, and battery life.)

Mashable tech reporter Alex Perry approved of the Pixel 11's performance, writing: "Apps load quickly and smoothly, on-device AI processing happens in a fairly snappy fashion, and the phone doesn't run all that hot, even without a case." Perry also called out the Pixel 11's new AI-powered Magic Capture image capture feature and Rambler text-to-speech tool, which wowed him even as a self-proclaimed AI skeptic. Unavailable on older Pixel phones, they alone make a decent case for upgrading to the Pixel 11.

iOS users on a budget: The iPhone 17e is the cheapest, most accessible, most low-stakes entry point into the world of Apple phones.

People who stash their phones in their pockets: The 6.1-inch iPhone 17e is shorter than the iPhone 17 as well as the ultra-thin, ultralight iPhone Air. It's not as light as the Air, but it's damn near close. It's the most compact traditional (non-flip or foldable) phone on this list.

Read Mashable's full review of the Apple iPhone 17e.

This spring, Apple refreshed its budget phone with MagSafe charging, more starting storage, and a more powerful chip (the same one inside the regular iPhone). The resulting iPhone 17e is a more convenient, future-proofed, and faster handset than before. It also takes slightly better photos in low-light settings.

While the standard iPhone 17 is a nicer device overall with vastly better cameras and a smoother display, the iPhone 17e is still a good, reliable phone for penny-pinchers who like iOS. It's a full $200 cheaper than its mid-tier counterpart, which is a significant difference for many shoppers.

People who want to venture beyond Apple, Samsung, and Google: Nothing is a British tech company that also makes stylish and affordable headphones and smartwatches. This affordable handset proves that the best smartphones don't have to cost you $1,000 and up.

Design enthusiasts: The Phone (4a) Pro sports the funky, retro-inspired look that Nothing has come to be known for.

People with the strictest budgets: Starting at $499 with 128GB of storage, this is the least expensive phone we recommend — now even more so after the iPhone 17e's recent price bump.

Read Mashable's full review of the Nothing (4a) Pro.

"If you want an under-$500 phone with flair," said Mashable contributor Adam Doud, "it doesn't get more flair-ish than" the Nothing Phone (4a) Pro. It has a striking retro-industrial look with a cool Glyph Matrix display on the back, which shows you the time, battery life, and other status indicators and notifications when it's face down. (Google just copied this feature, kind of.)

On the front, you'll find a surprisingly sharp AMOLED display with a top-tier 144Hz refresh rate. Its mid-range processor isn't fast enough to handle games, but it's apt for everyday usage scenarios and easy on its battery: "I regularly got just under two days of light-medium use on a single charge." Doud said. Google's identically priced Pixel 10a takes better pictures, but we think this is the better, snazzier budget Android phone overall.

Mobile photographers who prefer iOS: The iPhone 18 Pro takes fantastic photos in almost any environment, and it has much more customizable camera settings than lesser iPhones — including a physical variable aperture. (The iPhone 18 Pro Max has the same shooters, but it's much less portable.)

Folks who really like Apple's new burgundy color: The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are both available in the "dangerously chic" new hue, as Mashable's Shannon Connellan put it. This model will appeal to more people because it's slightly cheaper and more pocket-friendly.

Read Mashable's full review of the Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

Apple's latest Pro-tier handset has upgraded cameras with a new variable aperture on its main lens and new creator-friendly Pro controls. There are new Photographic Styles, new Cinematic video effects, and a new Focus Tracking tool, to name a few. All of these upgrades make the iPhone 18 Pro best-suited for serious shutterbugs who really like to fine-tune their camera settings, said Mashable senior editor Schroeder. "That doesn’t mean the regular user won't benefit," he wrote, "but I do bet that the majority of people will try out the manual aperture setting once and then leave it on auto."

Plus, the iPhone 18 Pro is configurable with up to 2TB of storage — it has plenty of room for all of your shots. Apple rounded out its spec sheet with a long battery life and a turbocharged A20 chip that gives it ample processing power for Siri AI.

Heads up: Early reviewers have reported some fading on the back of the burgundy and black iPhone 18 Pros, similar to the scratching problem with last year's cosmic orange iPhone 17 Pro. If that concerns you, either get a nice case or opt for the pretty new glacier blue iPhone 18 Pro instead. It doesn't seem to be having the same issue.

Mobile photographers who prefer Android: The Pixel 11 Pro takes the best photos of any Android phone we've tested. Not only are its cameras spectacular, but it also supports some great software features that make sure its pictures turn out great every time — Magic Capture, for one. (The standard Pixel 11 also has these features, though its cameras aren't quite as nice.)

Android users who want a high-end flagship with magnetic charging: Unlike the Samsung Galaxy S26 series, including the S26 Ultra, the Pixel 11 has built-in magnets. In other words, it supports magnetic charging by default. You don't need to buy a separate case to make sure it's securely attached to wireless chargers or accessories. (The regular Pixel 11 also has magnets, FWIW.)

Read Mashable's full review of the Google Pixel 11 Pro.

Admittedly, this category was a tight race between the Pixel 11 Pro and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. So, why did we pick the former? Take it from Mashable's Alex Perry: "Photography is fun on the Pixel 11 Pro, which is not something I feel about many handsets these days," he wrote. "A combination of hardware and software makes your images consistently look nice, even in challenging lighting conditions." Daytime shots, nighttime snaps, macro images, landscapes — in our experience, they all turn out great on the Pixel 11 Pro. Also worth noting: Google upgraded its digital zoom to a whopping 120x. (The Galaxy S26 Ultra's digital zoom maxes out at 100x.)

Cameras aside, we also gave high marks to this phone for its capable everyday performance, multi-day battery life, brighter display, and attractive color options. Its HiLight feature is kind of a flop, but the rest of it makes up for that.

Multitaskers on the move: The new iPhone Duo is thinner and lighter than Apple's iPads, and it has a huge, gorgeous inner display with a glare-reducing "nano-texture" finish. Its design makes it great for on-the-go multitasking and entertainment (think reading, watching movies, or playing games); it can replace an e-reader or tablet in a pinch.

Stylus users: The Duo is the only foldable we've tested that supports stylus input on its inner and outer displays. It works with the Apple Pencil (USB-C), which is sold separately for $79.

Early adopters: Foldable phones aren't in their infancy anymore, but they're still pretty niche devices. And as Apple's very first foldable, the Duo has some quirks — namely, many apps aren't optimized for it yet. Its ideal buyer is a tech enthusiast who wants to check out the latest and greatest in smartphone design and is willing to put up with some bugs for a bit.

People with cash to burn: The Duo starts at an eye-watering $1,999, making it Apple's most expensive phone ever — not to mention, the priciest phone on this list. (It maxes out at $3,199 with 2TB of storage.)

Patient people: The Duo was backordered for months at the time of writing. If you order it through the Apple Store right now, you probably won't get it until the opening weeks of 2027.

Read Mashable's full review of the Apple iPhone Duo.

The iPhone Duo is the first and only foldable that Apple's made so far, but it's quite impressive for a first-generation device. It's basically an iPhone that doubles as an iPad when unfolded — you can look at apps side by side, enjoy e-books and games in greater immersion, or use it as a MacBook's secondary display. (We just wouldn't recommend turning it into an alarm clock as Apple suggests.) It certainly helps that the Duo's matte inner screen is "the nicest phone display I’ve ever seen," said Senior Editor Stan Schroeder, who described it as "crisp, sharp, [and] beautiful to look at; it’s downright addictive."

The Duo has a passport-style design like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, our favorite Android foldable, just with rounder corners for a more polished look. It runs on the same powerful A20 chip as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, so it's zippy enough for all the multitasking your heart desires, and optimized apps work incredibly well. While the Duo doesn't last as long as those regular iPhones, its battery life is fine for a foldable.

You'll have to temper your expectations with the Duo's cameras — it lacks a telephoto lens, and the hidden FaceTime camera on its inner screen is straight-up "bad," Schroeder said. That said, this is the case with most foldables.

On a final note, some inaugural Duo owners reported that their device's inner screen cracked shortly after they started using it (a problem that's since become known as "crackgate"). The good news is that the issue doesn't seem to be as serious as social media might have you believe. In a statement, Apple told us that it's isolated to "a small number" of Duos, and that impacted buyers should contact AppleCare for a replacement.

If it helps, Schroeder has been using the Duo for nearly a month and hasn't noticed any hinge or display defects with his review unit. What's more, another Duo has withstood more than 200,000 folds (and counting) inside the "Fold-a-Phone" machine built by our sister site, CNET; they're folding it 900 times an hour until it breaks. You can catch the livestream daily on CNET's YouTube channel.

Commuters and frequent travelers: Like Apple's iPhone Duo, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 has a compact and versatile passport-style design that's tailor-made for multitasking on the go.

Reluctant guinea pigs: Unlike Apple, Samsung has been making foldable phones for many years now. Our reviewer noticed some "very minor bugs" with certain apps on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, but "most of the time, the phone just works," he said. And its construction is pretty much rock solid at this point. (We think the iPhone Duo's "crackgate" issue is largely overblown, but it's still something to be aware of.)

People who like a lightweight foldable: This is the lightest folding phone we've tested. It's 21 percent lighter than the iPhone Duo, 16 percent lighter than the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and six percent lighter than Samsung's taller, book-style Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

Folks who want an "affordable" foldable: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is $100 cheaper than Apple's iPhone Duo. If we're really splitting hairs, it's technically the thriftier choice.

Read Mashable's full review of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8.

Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold is also a great Android foldable, but ultimately, we prefer the wider, passport-style design of Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 — it's sleeker and better for entertainment. Plus, its crease isn't as visible. (We also prefer it over the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra for similar reasons.)

The Galaxy Z Fold 8's spacious inner AMOLED screen is "far and away" its biggest asset, said Mashable's Timothy Beck Werth. It's smooth and so bright. "I generally avoid streaming TV shows and movies on my phone, but not with the Z Fold 8," he wrote. "Likewise, while I've never been a huge fan of mobile gaming, the mobile version of Mario Kart looks and plays awesome here."

The display has a glare-free finish that makes it easy to view in direct sunlight, as well as Samsung's new "Flex Titanium" tech that keeps its crease subtle and hinge strong. Other highlights of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 include peppy multitasking performance and all-day battery life. While its cameras aren't spectacular — most foldables' shooters aren't — they're sufficient for most non-pro users.

The most advanced iPhone ever built is here, and it doesn't disappoint. So, who should buy the iPhone 18 Pro Max instead of the smaller iPhone 18 Pro?

Battery life maximizers: The iPhone 18 Pro Max is rated for up to 45 hours of video playback. It's the longest-lasting phone we've ever tested.

Mobile gamers who prefer regular (non-foldable) phones: This handset features a blazing-fast processor and a huge vapor chamber thermal system, plus a smooth, crisp, and massive display.

People with big hands: At 8.78 ounces, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the heaviest regular phone we recommend. It's the same size as the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, but weighs 16 percent more.

Read Mashable's full review of the Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

Apple reorganized the components inside the iPhone 18 Pro Max to squeeze in a giant new battery that can run for nearly two days between charges. It's so big that the company had to add a special setting that keeps it within shipping limits on battery sizes. It lasts up to nine hours longer than the smaller iPhone 18 Pro, no "Max."

The iPhone 18 Pro Max's A20 Pro chip ran laps around the competition in our benchmarking, and the new thermal management system that fills its chassis keeps it cool while you're running demanding apps. Mashable's Stan Schroeder "tested this out by playing a few games of PUBG: Battlegrounds on the highest settings for a full hour," and "The phone barely got warm," he wrote. Its battery life only fell by nine percent during that stress test, FWIW.

The regular iPhone 18 Pro has the same hardware, but we think mobile gamers and movie-watchers will appreciate the bigger, more immersive screen on the "Max" version. The two phones are basically identical otherwise, including their shooter setup. Opt for this model if you want the best iPhone for battery life and cameras.

"If there's ever been a phone to make you ditch Apple, this is it," said Mashable tech editor Timothy Beck Werth. The question is, who should make the splurge?

Advanced users: The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra is a premium device with a zippy custom processor, a large, high-end display with stylus support, and elite cameras. It's "too much phone" for the average person, to quote our review; only professional creatives and developers will be able to use it to its full potential.

AI enthusiasts: This handheld comes crammed with powerful AI tools, including pre-loaded Gemini, Perplexity, and Bixby AI assistants.

Read Mashable's full review of the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra.

In October, Samsung raised the prices of the Galaxy S26 phones it released back in March — and they were already more expensive than last year's S25 models. A new S26 Ultra will now cost you $1,400, while the 1TB version is a whopping $2,000. But if you want the finest, most future-proofed Android smartphone available, this is it.

Teens with deep-pocketed parents: The trendy little Galaxy Z Flip 8 makes a great starter phone for a younger person (though it doesn't have a "starter" price). It's cute, durable, and easy to hold in one hand.

People who don't obsess over photo quality: Like foldables, flip phones aren't ideal for serious photographers. The Galaxy Z Flip 8's cameras underwhelm compared to those on regular phones that cost the same or slightly less.

Nostalgic Millennials: If you haven't used a flip phone since the early 2000s, this is a great entry point into the modern market.

Read Mashable's full review of the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8.

In addition to your usual next-gen upgrades — a faster processor, a slightly thinner, lighter design — the Galaxy Z Flip 8 also features improved durability compared to last year's Galaxy Z Flip 7. Like the Galaxy Z Fold 8, above, its new Flex Titanium display tech equates to a stronger hinge and a more subtle crease on its inner screen. Mashable tech editor Timothy Beck Werth was particularly enamored by its small size and "charming good looks," calling it "a smartphone with good vibes."

Its color options are few but cute; the pink one won over our newsroom full of Apple users. While its cameras aren't much to write home about as a whole, it takes great selfies (as long as you don't use the selfie camera, ironically), and its AI image editing tools work really well. Regarding battery life, you should get over a day of use out of the Z Flip 8 before needing to charge it.

People who want a flip phone with great cameras: Flip phones aren't known for taking amazing pictures — Samsung's Galaxy Z Flip 8, above, is pretty representative of the market — but this model is an exception.

Folks who want a long-lasting flip phone: The latest Razr Ultra can last up to a day and a half away from an outlet, depending on your usage.

Fashionistas: This flip phone comes in two chic, Pantone-approved colorways featuring unique back covers.

If you can spend a little more on your flip phone, we really like the 2026 Motorola Razr Ultra, which Mashable tech editor Timothy Beck Werth deemed "a conversation-starting beauty." Both of its pretty AMOLED displays (inner and outer) are bigger, smoother, and brighter than the ones on last year's model.

Its external design is equally eye-catching: The Pantone Orient Blue model's cover is finished in Alcantara, a suede-like microfiber, while the Pantone Cocoa one has a wood veneer on the back. It takes "surprisingly good photos for a foldable," Werth said — better than the Galaxy Z Flip 8 for sure — capturing natural-looking colors and handling bright scenes well. Its 36-hour battery life is also an improvement over its Samsung counterpart, which taps out at 31 hours (same with the mid-tier Razr+, which also underwhelmed in the photography department).
